findings.passage: Sankar tells both of his early career decisions the same way. He wanted the risky option, and his father made the call.
findings.problem: Colossus supports this for Xoom only, and weakly. There the father, who "had been kind of trying not to be directive", told him to take the job he "badly" wanted. For Palantir the source shows no ruling by his father at all. Stern reports that he had grown restless at Xoom ("he felt he wasn't learning enough and that the company wasn't growing fast enough"), met Lonsdale through a friend, and decided after the interviews: "I was kind of ruined ... there was no going back." "Once again it was a fork in the road where Dad was right" credits the earlier advice; it does not report an instruction. The H2 "The two forks his father decided", the line "told as obedience" and the FAQ's "He credits his biggest choices to his father" turn one anecdote into a pattern. The draft also leaves out that he quit his first employer after about two years because it had stopped feeding him, which cuts against a loyalty-first reading. Evidence claims C11 and C64 repeat the error.
findings.acceptance_test: The section says that only the Xoom choice involved his father's ruling, that the ruling backed what he already wanted, and that he chose Palantir himself after growing restless at Xoom. The H2, the "obedience" sentence, the type FAQ line and claims C11/C64 are rewritten or cut to match. No sentence states or implies that his father decided the Palantir move.

findings.passage: Both times he forecast failure, carried it up to the one person he trusted, and came away steadier.
findings.problem: The evidence record calls this the main discriminator against Type 8 (C14, C71), and the sources do not carry it. (1) In both tellings of the 2008 call he gives his own cause, which the draft cuts: "I called him incredibly grumpy. Humorless from sleep deprivation" (Hudson transcript); "I was so sleep deprived, I got super fucking grumpy and humorless" (Colossus). Colossus places the call after the analysts had "declared the product useful", so this was not a moment that was going wrong. (2) Neither source says he came away steadier. He says "And I was shocked"; Colossus says Karp "felt so vindicated". "The one person he trusted" appears nowhere. (3) The draft writes that the laugh "felt like 10 minutes," because Karp "understood"; his stated reason is "in my humorless mood". (4) He tells the second story to show Karp's jokes, and "freaking out at him ... How did you sign us up for this work?" is a subordinate berating his boss, which suits Type 8 as well as Type 6. (5) He was a team lead in his twenties phoning the chief executive. Rank explains "carried it up" for any type. (6) Of the same deployment he told O'Shaughnessy "I was leading the deployment. It was all on me" (S08, Whisper clip at 24:15), which sits badly beside "He does not describe taking over."
findings.acceptance_test: The section quotes his sleep-deprivation explanation and says the customer had just approved the product. "The one person he trusted" and "came away steadier" are cut unless a source says so. The rank confound and "It was all on me" are stated in the body. The two anecdotes are no longer presented as the deciding evidence against Type 8, and the Why-not-8 bullet, the FAQ line "he describes taking alarm to Karp in a crisis" and C71 are scaled to match.

findings.passage: In twenty years he has not left or started a company of his own, though he calls Palantir "a founder factory"
findings.problem: The profile's main source says otherwise. Colossus reports "He'd started a movie studio" and quotes him on "starting a movie studio around the American cinematic universe". His September 2024 House biography (S19) says he chairs the board of Ginkgo Bioworks and launched the First Breakfast initiative in 2023. The research packet held the film company (former C37); the draft cut it and then asserted the opposite. The linked claim that he has been "one man's deputy since 2006" (description, Why-not-8 FAQ, first Why-not-8 bullet) is the article's construction. Colossus says he joined as the 13th employee, "originally hired to lead 'business development'", and was named chief operating officer by February 2021. The evidence record admits the title history is thin (C01, C114). These two statements carry the tenure argument and feed the type hypothesis through C20.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence is corrected to what the record shows: he has not left Palantir, and while staying he started a film studio and a publishing venture and chaired another public company's board, each sourced and dated. "Deputy since 2006" is removed from the description, the FAQ and the bullet, or replaced with a dated and sourced account of his roles. C20 and C114 are corrected.

findings.passage: Margaret Brennan asked about a February 2026 U.S. strike that hit a school in Minab, Iran, and a Bloomberg report that Pentagon personnel had relied too much on Palantir's Maven system.
findings.problem: The question as aired said the strike "killed at least 123 school children" (captions at 15:03; the Whisper clip the record used for this exchange opens with those words). The cited Gizmodo article reports "more than 150 people, including at least 123 children". The draft removes the deaths from both, so a reader cannot weigh "the likely cause is human error" or "Sadly, I'm just a technologist". C92 says the passage states "the question as put on the broadcast". It does not. The paragraph also omits the rest of what makes the exchange adverse. Asked again, he confirmed he meant human error and not overreliance on the AI. Asked about briefing Congress on what went wrong, he said "I would defer to the department on that. That's not our place" (captions at 16:57, not checked by ear). He said Palantir then built added checks "to ensure things like that couldn't happen again". The Bloomberg article itself was not opened by research or by me.
findings.acceptance_test: The passage gives the death toll with attribution (Brennan's on-air figure and the Gizmodo count of Bloomberg's reporting, noting that counts vary). The paragraph includes the "not our place" answer and the post-strike fix beside his denial. C92's inference is corrected. The caption-only wording is checked by ear or paraphrased.

findings.passage: He is also specific about where the license ends.
findings.problem: The section reads three deferrals as temperament. Each came when responsibility for Palantir's product or his own conflict was the question. The "unelected engineers" line answered Stern's questions about ICE detentions and whether such tools should exist; the draft strips that context, as it does for the "cultures are corrupt" quote from the same exchange, where his indignation was aimed at the argument for restraining institutions. The CBS deferrals came on a strike that killed children. The "lawyers" line came on his own conflict of interest. Where deference would cost him, the record shows assertion, and the draft omits it. Palantir sued the Army in 2016 and won (Colossus), which is the "break with authority after being overruled" the Why-not-8 section says is absent. He has testified to Congress and published a reform treatise and a book on rewriting procurement. Colossus calls him "a regular at The White House" and says he wrote on why he aligned behind Trump. In the same CBS interview he assigned liability to AI companies and argued for an incident-reporting regime before saying "I'm just a technologist". Moments before the line the draft paraphrases, he tells Lonsdale that being a heretic means sacrifice "at the expense of your career" (captions at 27:05), which is not "a loyalist with a sponsor". The draft concedes the incentive reading only for the product defense on Minab.
findings.acceptance_test: The section gives the question each deferral answered. It states the incentive explanation (deference is the cheap answer when accountability is raised) as a live alternative for all three. It adds the 2016 Army suit and his policy advocacy as evidence against a deference pattern. The Why-not-8 claim that the record shows no break with authority is revised to account for the suit, or scoped to his personal conduct with that limit stated. "A loyalist with a sponsor" is kept only if squared with his own "expense of your career" gloss.

findings.passage: Read plainly, the sentence says safety was granted by something bigger than the family, and that it is owed for.
findings.problem: The article's central causal story rests on a sentence whose surrounding account shifts, and the body does not say so. In December 2024 he said "my family came to this country as refugees fleeing violence from Nigeria" (School of War transcript). Colossus reports that the family left Lagos for India and came to Orlando when a childhood friend offered his father work: "You've got nothing to lose. It would be a good way to start over." In October 2025, asked about Palantir and mass deportations, he said "we came here legally" (captions at 33:41, not checked by ear). On the Colossus account the United States did not take the family out of Lagos, so the sentence works as a family creed more than a description of events. "Owed for" is the draft's addition. In the same passage the father's attitude is given as "We survived what happened in Nigeria, we can survive anything" and "Grateful is the word". The record notes the refugee/legal discrepancy (C04, C113), and the draft confines it to one FAQ clause.
findings.acceptance_test: The body reports the three versions with dates and sources, including the return to India and the job offer. It presents "dead in a ditch in Lagos" as a creed he repeats and not as the route the family took. "Owed for" is marked as the author's inference from his later "give back" statements, with the father's "we can survive anything" quoted beside it. The parents FAQ matches the body.

findings.passage: That is the strongest evidence against a Six reading, and it deserves to be taken at face value before anyone argues with it.
findings.problem: The draft argues with it in the next sentence and never says what the face-value reading implies. "One way to hear that is as a Six describing a base that held" lets a denial of fear count as evidence of fear, so no answer he gave could have counted against the type. The same Colossus passages hold more that points away from fear, all omitted: "It never fazed Dad"; the Westerns he and his father acted out, which he glosses as "You're alone and not afraid ... it's still important to be a hero and not a coward"; and shame language that outweighs the fear language (the process server was "humiliating" before "terrifying", his mother bagging groceries was "embarrassing", the misprinted T-shirts, "Why not me?"). That shame material belongs to Type 3, which the draft dismisses with "two decades out of public view". His own 2024 House biography (S19) calls him "A frequent guest on CNBC and Bloomberg" and dates First Breakfast to 2023, he gave a TED talk in June 2012, and Colossus quotes "Please don't let my tombstone just read 'defense tech'". The evidence record says Type 3 cannot be ruled out. The draft says only that it was "tested".
findings.acceptance_test: A paragraph states the face-value reading and which types it favours, and includes the "alone and not afraid" and "never fazed Dad" material. The "base that held" line is labelled as a reading this record cannot test, and the article says what observation would count against fear as the core emotion. The Type 3 paragraph drops "two decades out of public view" for a sourced statement of his lower profile before late 2024, adds the shame and tombstone evidence, and says Type 3 remains live.

findings.passage: And he still describes his place as something he has to earn every day.
findings.problem: The hook's quotation is cut before the clause that fixes its meaning. The full sentence (Whisper clip and captions at 28:42) is "you carry that chip on your shoulder to like earn your place every day and you recognize your product has to be 10 times better than the alternatives". He says it about "the beginning of Palantir", when "we tried to go through the front door". He is describing the early company's position against incumbents, in the past, and "you" is the company. The evidence record admits this in C48's alternative. The draft still turns it into a present-tense personal confession, and the type hypothesis lists C48 as support. Only "Constitutionally, I'm going to always feel like an outsider" and the "heretic looking in" lines are personal and present-tense.
findings.acceptance_test: The quotation runs through "10 times better than the alternatives" or is introduced as a remark about early Palantir. The sentence saying he "still describes his place as something he has to earn every day" is cut or rebuilt on the outsider lines alone. C48 is removed from the type hypothesis's supporting claims or reclassified as a statement about the company.

findings.passage: He still concluded that "his message is important, and he does actually believe it."
findings.problem: Stern's verdict is quoted without the doubt he attaches to it. He writes that in this media world sincerity and "the knowing performance of it have become practically indistinguishable", and that audiences may not tell "genuine warnings" from "a rhetorically sophisticated strategy for business development". That is the skeptic's case, made by the draft's own witness, and the draft drops it. The sources are also less separate than the citations suggest. The Colossus profile and Invest Like the Best share a publisher, and the podcast hosted him weeks after the profile ran. The gala and the April 2026 book talk were Hudson Institute events, and Hudson's event page describes him as a Hudson trustee at the time of the gala. Lonsdale hired him. The evidence record notes the first two relationships (S01, S11). The limits paragraph names ally witnesses but not ally venues.
findings.acceptance_test: The public-turn section quotes or closely paraphrases Stern's business-development caveat beside his verdict. The limits section states the Colossus/podcast and Hudson relationships in a sentence.

findings.passage: No court ruled on the claims, and no statement from Sankar about the case has been found.
findings.problem: The i2 allegation is reported with care and then kept away from every argument it bears on. The heretic section defines his rule-breaking as done "for the institution, by someone inside it, with cover from above". The complaint, per VentureBeat, alleged that software was "fraudulently obtained" under his parents' company name and that the conduct ran four years, which would be a rule broken against an outsider. The Karp section lets "completely honest" stand with no pointer to the one allegation of misrepresentation on record. The evidence record draws both connections and notes the episode would favour Type 8 if accurate (C21, C33). The draft draws neither and omits the alleged duration.
findings.acceptance_test: One conditional sentence in the type argument says what the allegation would mean for the "loyalist" reading and the 6-versus-8 call if it were accurate, without asserting that it is. The honesty anecdote notes that an unresolved allegation of misrepresentation sits beside it. The alleged four-year span is stated with attribution to VentureBeat's account of the complaint.

protected_passages.passage: Loyalty and money point the same way here, so the tenure cannot settle the type alone.
protected_passages.reason: States the incentive confound at the point where the loyalty argument is strongest, using the proxy figures. This is the standard the rest of the type case should meet.

protected_passages.passage: Almost all of this is Sankar's own retelling, polished across at least ten long interviews in 2025 and 2026 by an executive whose company benefits from a grateful-patriot story.
protected_passages.reason: The plainest statement of the evidence problem in the article, and accurate to the record. Keep it, and move its logic up into the sections it limits.

protected_passages.passage: What would move the read toward Eight: accounts of him overriding or walking away from Karp or the Army at a cost to himself, or people outside his circle describing domination for its own sake.
protected_passages.reason: Names concrete disconfirming evidence in reader language. Rare in type writing and worth keeping even if the discriminator around it is rebuilt.

protected_passages.passage: Lonsdale had just described the early Palantir as outsiders beaten up by the bureaucracy, so part of that answer is a guest agreeing with his host.
protected_passages.reason: Limits the hook with its real context before the article builds on it. Checked against the captions and Whisper clip at 28:00.

protected_passages.passage: The limits are real. Mabrey's line is his reading of Sankar's motive, and everyone describing this style thrived under it. An invitation to curse at the boss is still the boss's game.
protected_passages.reason: Separates a colleague's inference from Sankar's motive and names the survivorship problem in the testimony. Matches Colossus, where Mabrey says "He just thinks".

assessment:
Read as a fair-minded skeptic. I reopened the thesis-bearing and adverse sources by live fetch on 2026-10-13: the Colossus profile (read in full), the Hudson gala transcript, VentureBeat via the Wayback Machine, Gizmodo, Military.com and the Revolving Door Project page. For the Lonsdale, O'Shaughnessy, Douthat and CBS interviews, the School of War transcript and the House biography I read the run's saved captions, Whisper clips and text. I did not open the Bloomberg investigation, the i2 complaint or any official broadcast transcript, so the caption-only wording I cite is not confirmed by ear.

The draft is more candid than most. It names the ally-only witness pool, prints the i2 allegation, the Minab exchange and the recusal story, sets money beside loyalty, and says what would move the read to Eight. Every quotation I checked matched its source word for word.

The weakness is what happens to each adverse item after it is disclosed. Minab runs without its dead. The "democracy" and "cultures are corrupt" quotes lose the ICE and surveillance questions that prompted them. The i2 allegation and the refugee/legal shift are parked away from the arguments they bear on. Meanwhile three supports of the Six-over-Eight case do not survive the sources: his father decided one fork, not two; the crisis call was sleep-deprived grumpiness after a success, and "came away steadier" is the draft's; "earn your place every day" was about the early company's product. A fourth, that he never started a company of his own, is contradicted by the main source. The deference section reads as temperament a pattern that incentives explain as well, and it omits Palantir's 2016 suit against the Army.

With those repaired, what remains for Six over Eight is long tenure (confounded by money, as the draft says), a gala tribute and one colleague's gloss. Six may still be the best reading, but medium confidence has to be re-argued on what is left. If no discriminator can be rebuilt, the honest outcome under the standard is insufficient_evidence with the non-ally testimony task. A twenty-year record rules out an open case. If repair changes the type or the thesis, the run needs --refresh --expanded-review.

Similarity: not tripped (maximum 0.058). The matched lines are ordinary counterphobic-Six vocabulary, and the details here (Shyam Bombs, the parole officer line, the Lagos sentence) belong to this subject. The diagnostic suggests the Bryan, Burr and Mensch pages also argue a "looks like an Eight, tests whether it holds" Six. I was given only the diagnostic and could not compare the full arguments, so I raise no finding on reuse.
